content.title: Thank you very much for your time and constructive feedback.
content.comment: We sincerely appreciate the careful review and constructive comments from the reviewers. Given the comments, we are clarifying the motivation and contribution of our work on “layer-wise balanced activation” and conducting experiments on additional datasets such as ImageNet to validate our work more clearly and broadly. However, the two-week-period for revision and rebuttal seems short to complete these improvements. Thus, unfortunately, we think we have to withdraw our work for ICLR 2023. We will show the contribution and validity of our work through other opportunities. Again, we thank the reviewers very much for their time and constructive feedback.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new mechanism called LayerAct to measure the imbalanced activation problem in neural network training. The authors discuss the imbalanced distribution of activations introduces bias during training, which harms network optimization and reduces model performance. Inspired by LayerNorm, the authors propose a LayerAct mechanism, which normalizes the input of activation scale with sample statistics. The proposed LayerAct makes ResNets converge faster and achieves higher top-1 accuracy than ReLU and SiLU on CIFAR.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1.	The authors summarize a new formulation of activation function as a=y*s(y), where function s(y) is the activation scale. Based on this formulation, LayerAct can effectively normalize the imbalance activation inputs without trainable parameters.
2.	The normalization mechanism in LayerAct effectively speeds up network convergence.

Weakness:
1.	Section 4.1 is confusing. The authors do not sufficiently explain the relationship between activation scale and training loss. It is difficult to understand how imbalanced activation influences network training from Section 4.1 and Figure 2. I suggest the authors improve this part to convince readers that resolving the imbalance activation phenomenon is meaningful.
2.	The accuracy improvements over ReLU and SiLU are marginal. These results are not supported to be published at this conference.
3.	Writing issue. Equation 4 lost H in mean and std; In Figure 2, the axis labels are overlapped, and pictures are not aligned; The captions of tables and figures should be clear for easy understanding.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed LayerAct introduces a normalization mechanism in non-linearity to achieve faster convergence during model training. But the improvements of LayerAct are marginal, and the explanations are insufficient to understand how the imbalance activations phenomenon influence model training. I suggest the authors keep in touch with the latest papers about activation functions to improve this work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new activation function (LayerAct) to enable layer-wise balanced activation, such that the deep models converges faster and achieves better performance. The paper show that the training loss is related to the sum of the activation scale. The findings indicate that imbalanced activation scale of samples could lead to learning bias. Moreover, the proposed LayerAct allows negative activation, outperform some element-level activation functions on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
(1)	The paper proposes a new activation function.
(2)	the proposed LayerAct improves the performance on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.


Weakness:

(1)	The paper claims that most of the existing activation functions have an element-level activation mechanism and lead to imbalanced distributions of activation. It is unclear why we need balanced distributions. Take a classification task as an example, the goal is to extract helpful features for classification. Given an image, the networks need to extract helpful features and filter unavailable features (e.g., background). Some samples could contain more unavailable features. Therefore, the activation could be imbalanced. The motivation of imbalanced activation distribution is not clear.
(2)	The experiments of the paper are insufficient. The paper only performs experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100. ImageNet-1k should be added. The paper only compares ReLU, which misses lots of activation functions. The paper is far from effectively validated.
(3)	In figure 3, the figure does not show a faster convergence than other element-level activation functions. Simply scaling the training losses by 0.0001 also leads to small training loss values.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper proposes a new activation loss for image classification. However, the paper does not perform the evaluation experiments such as large-scale datasets and comparisons to more activations. The motivation of balanced activation distributions is unclear. Overall, the evaluation experiments do not strongly support the advantages of the proposed activation function.
content.summary_of_the_review:
(1) The motivation of balanced activation distributions is unclear.
(2) The paper does not perform the evaluation experiments such as large-scale datasets and comparisons to more activations.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a new activation mechanism called layer-wise balanced activation (LayerAct). The authors claim that it can address the imbalanced distribution of activation while maintaining a diverse distribution of activation. Experiment results on CIFAR10/CIFAR100 are provided to support the proposed opinion.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:

1. Table 1 and Figure 1 clearly illustrate the difference between LayerAct and other methods.

Cons:

1. The improvement of the proposed LayerAct is marginal. As shown in Table 2, under the standard CNN with BN settings, the improvements of LA-SiLU and LA_HardSiLU are 0.03 and 0.06 over the SiLU and HardSiLU, respectively, in terms of the mean accuracy. This improvement is far smaller than the deviation according to the large gap between the best and the mean accuracies.

2. The explanation of Figure 2 is confusing. Where are the positive and negative relationships? And How could this lead to the bias?

3. For the statement: "LayerNorm loses the mean and variance statistics of activated instances among samples during re-scaling and re-centering." Why is this a problem?

4. The performance of the CNN-LN is too low to believe. Did the author tune the hyperparameters? I believe studying networks where LN has been widely used (e.g. ViT) can be more convincing.

6. The study on large-scale dataset (e.g. ImageNet) is required.

7. In Figure 2, The label y-axis is clipped in some subplots.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Fair. (Some explanations are confusing.) 

Quality: Fair. (requires further improvement as discussed in Cons)

Novelty: Good. (I didn't see this technique before)

Reproducibility: Fair. (Releasing the code can further improve the reproducibility)

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper claims that the imbalanced activation phenomenon among samples induces a bias in the training of a network against samples. It also claims that layer normalization (LayerNorm) can be used to avoid such problem but loses all the mean and variance statistics of linear projection. It thus proposes an activation function, LayerAct, that combines the idea of layer normalization and sigmoid linear units. Several preliminary experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR100 datasets show the performance improvement of LayerAct over several baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**

The proposed LayerAct has potentiality to improve the performance of the current MLP, CNN architectures, based on the preliminary experimental results. 

**Weaknesses:**

1. I have concerns on the main claims of this paper. This paper claims the imbalanced activation phenomenon among samples, as stated “As such, the element-level activation mechanism of backpropagation induces a bias in the training of a network against samples; more parameters in the network are fitted to some training samples more than others”. And this phenomenon induces a bias in the training of a network against samples. Does this phenomenon harm the training of neural networks or degenerate the performance? It is not clear how this phenomenon harm the training of a network. The only support is from a preliminary experiment shown in Section 4.1 on MNIST using MLP, showing there is a correlation between the sum of activation scale and training loss while training the network, but what kind of correlation is not further showed (positive negative, does strictly related?). 
Intuitively, It is important that the network can well differ the difficult or easy examples, that is It is OK for different examples have different values of their activations/gradients. 

2. The proposed LayerAct is LayerNorm + (genearal) sigmoid-linear-units in native. Both of them are good methods in improving the performance of neural network. I think the technical contribution is overall low, and the novelty is incremental. 

3. The experimental results are preliminary. 1) the baselines of the proposed method should include the comparison to not only the advanced nonlinear-activation functions, but also the advanced normalization techniques, since this paper is a combination of LayerNorm and (general) sigmoid-linear-units; 2) This paper should conduct experiments on large-scale ImageNet experiments.

4. This paper should provide a section of related work about normalization techniques, and discuss the recent normalization techniques and show the difference and advantages. 

The paper has many imprecise parts, here are a few:

(1)In the abstract, “LayerNorm loses the mean and variance statistics of activated instances among samples during re-scaling and re-centering.” What is the meaning of “re-scaling” and re-centering? Are they the corresponding mean-subtract and variance-divide operations?  If yes, one should use the term center/centering and scale/scaling as described in the original BN paper, not the so-called “re-centering” and “re-scaling”.

 (2)As the definition of the MLP, what is the differences between the x^l and a^l, how does eqn.1 describe an MLP? 

(3)In Section 2, does N($b^l$, $g^{l^2}$) means a Gaussian distribution with mean $b^l$ and variance  $g^{l^2}$? If yes, I believe this is wrong, because fixing the mean and variance only does not mean a distribution will be a Gaussian.

 (4)In Fig.2, what is the dashed line meaning? What is the solid line meaning? This paper should provide necessary illustration for reading to understanding the meaning of the figures. 

 (5)What is the meaning of “LayerNorm loses all the mean and variance statistics of linear projection”? I think LayerNorm only fix the mean as 0 and variance as 1, but does not lose all the mean and variance statistics
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity is somewhat unclear and I have concerns on the main claims, the quality and novelty is somewhat low. I don’t think the experiments can be well reproduced based on the descriptions of this paper, I think reproducible code should be provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: I vote to reject this paper since its unclear clarification of claims, low quality in presentation and incremental novelty.

content.title: Layer-wise Balanced Activation Mechanism
content.abstract: We propose a novel activation mechanism called LayerAct mechanism to develop layer-wise balanced activation functions that converge faster and perform better than existing activation functions. During the backpropagation in neural networks, the scale of activation function determines how much the parameters will be trained using each sample. This fact indicates that training of a neural network can be biased against samples when the distribution of activation is imbalanced among samples. With a simple experiment on the unnormalized network with rectified linear units (ReLUs) for activation, we show that there is a relationship between the sum of the activation scale and the training loss, which indicates that an imbalanced activation scale among samples can result in a bias in learning. The layer normalization (LayerNorm) can be used to avoid such problems of bias in learning by balancing the layer-wise distribution of inputs for activation functions. However, LayerNorm loses the mean and variance statistics of activated instances among samples during re-scaling and re-centering. Our proposed LayerAct mechanism balances the layer-wise distribution of activation outputs for all samples without re-scaling and re-centering; this way, LayerAct functions avoid not only the problem of bias in learning, but also the dilution problem of key statistics. LayerAct functions allow negative activation outputs when the activated signals have to be negative; thus, the machine can avoid bias shifts during learning, enabling rich representations at the end. Moreover, the proposed LayerAct mechanism can be used with the batch normalization (BatchNorm). Experiments show that LayerAct functions outperform the unbalanced element-level activation functions on two benchmark image classification datasets, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100. Given the essential role of activation in traditional multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and modern deep learning frameworks, our original work on the layer-wise activation fundamentally addressing the core mechanism of learning through multiple layers will contribute in developing high-performance machine learning frameworks.
